1	We have all seen the photos: birds nesting in piles of garbage along the shore, fish fatally caught
     2	in discarded netting, and huge mosaics of debris floating in the ocean. Even more alarmingly, what
     3	we see in these poignant images is only a portion of the problem. Approximately half of all plastic
     4	pollution is submerged below the ocean surface, much of it in the form of microplastics so small
     5	that we may never be able to clean them up completely.
     6	
     7	To cut through the enormity of the ocean pollution crisis, one approach is to focus on something
     8	recognizable within these images of debris. Identify something you personally have used that may
     9	have ended up in the oceanâ€”a water bottle perhaps. Find one in an image and ask yourself, how did
    10	it get there?
    11	
    12	Plastic is a human-made, synthetic material that was first discovered more than one hundred years
    13	ago but did not broadly enter the public sphere until the 1950s. While currently a major culprit in
    14	ocean pollution, plastics are not inherently bad for humans or the environment. In fact, in a United
    15	Nations (UN) report on combatting the negative effects of plastics, the head of the UN Environment
    16	Programme Erik Solheim made a point to acknowledge that plastic is in fact a â€œmiracle material.â€
    17	
    18	â€œThanks to plastics, countless lives have been saved in the health sector, the growth of clean
    19	energy from wind turbines and solar panels has been greatly facilitated, and safe food storage has
    20	been revolutionized,â€ Solheim wrote in his introduction. Yet plastic bottles are one of the most
    21	common items within marine debris. So how did such a promising material become a symbol of human
    22	environmental desecration?
    23	
    24	Plastic bottles are a single-use plastic, a product designed to be used only once and then
    25	discarded. Single-use plastics also include plastic packaging, for example of meats and fresh
    26	produce, which accounts for almost half of all plastic pollution. This type of plastic product is
    27	distinct from multi-use plastics, which can also pollute the ocean, but tend to amass less
    28	frequently due to their multi-use nature.
    29	
    30	For example, refillable bottles can store water in a way that does not produce the repeated waste of
    31	a single-use plastic water bottle. Refillable bottles can be made of many materials, including
    32	plastic, but last much longer than a single-use bottle and can be recycled when they become old or
    33	damaged. For both types of bottles, how they are discarded determines their ultimate resting place
    34	and whether they become pollutants of the ocean.
    35	
    36	A single-use plastic water bottle was manufactured, filled with water, and likely transported to a
    37	store, where it sat on a shelf waiting for a thirsty purchaser. Many of us drink out of plastic
    38	bottles several times during an average day, week, or month. Once we are finished with it, we have a
    39	choice where we leave that bottle:
    40	
    41	Recycling bin: Bottles destined for recycling are unlikely to end up in the ocean, in their current
    42	form, unless they are mismanaged or lost in transit to a processing facility. However, due to recent
    43	limitations in how recyclables are internationally transferred and accepted for processing, many of
    44	these bottles will unfortunately end up in landfills rather than recycling facilities.
    45	Trash can: These bottles also will not likely end up, in their current form, in the ocean. However,
    46	in areas across the globe with poor waste management or a lack of properly sealed landfills, as a
    47	bottle breaks down into microplastic particles over time, some particles may seep into the soil and
    48	eventually make their way into our waterways, ultimately entering and polluting the ocean.
    49	Litter: These bottles may very well be carried by wind, storm water, or other processes to sewers,
    50	rivers, lakes, and other waterways that may ultimately deposit the bottle in the ocean.
    51	Multi-use plastic bottles face these same pathways at end of their lifeâ€”but of course this happens
    52	much less frequently since they can be used many times.
    53	
    54	National Geographic Explorer Heather J. Koldewey works to empower communities around the world to
    55	participate in solving the ocean pollution crisis from single-use plastics via incremental
    56	individual actionsâ€”including a campaign called One Less, which encourages people to stop using
    57	single-use plastic water bottles altogether. One Less is currently based in and focused on London,
    58	England and its inhabitants, but anyone can make the choice to use one less single-use bottle.

Based solely on `doc.txt`, the document lists the following pros of plastic (and, by extension, plastic bottles):

**Pros of plastic in general:**
- Plastics are "not inherently bad for humans or the environment."
- The head of the UN Environment Programme, Erik Solheim, called plastic a "miracle material."
- "Thanks to plastics, countless lives have been saved in the health sector."
- "The growth of clean energy from wind turbines and solar panels has been greatly facilitated."
- "Safe food storage has been revolutionized."

**Regarding plastic bottles specifically:**
The document does not explicitly list pros of single-use plastic bottles. It notes that many people drink out of plastic bottles several times a day, and that plastic bottles are a "promising material" product. However, it does highlight benefits of **refillable (multi-use) plastic bottles**:
- They can store water in a way that does not produce the repeated waste of a single-use plastic water bottle.
- They last much longer than a single-use bottle.
- They can be recycled when they become old or damaged.

The document's overall framing is that plastic is a beneficial "miracle material," but that single-use plastic bottles—designed to be used once and discarded—are among the most common items in marine debris.
